channel.title: Mulder, It's Me
channel.description: Essays on The X-Files as film and television craft.

item.title: Series Order: What Hulu Actually Bought
item.description: Eight months after ordering a pilot, Hulu has picked up Ryan Coogler's X-Files to series. Sorting the confirmed from the reported from the rumored, and what the shape of the deal says about the show.

item.title: After the Basement: How The X-Files Rewired Television
item.description: A procedural with a serialized conspiracy underneath, a writers' room that became a showrunner academy, and a look that prestige TV absorbed. Tracing what the show left behind.

item.title: I Want to Believe, Reconsidered
item.description: Released in July 2008 a week after The Dark Knight, the second X-Files film was dismissed as small and strange. Seen now, its smallness looks like the point.

item.title: The Actors Behind the Camera
item.description: David Duchovny wrote and directed The Unnatural and Hollywood A.D. Gillian Anderson wrote and directed all things. What the show's two leads chose to make when they took control.

item.title: Scoring the Unseen: Mark Snow's Electronic Dread
item.description: Mark Snow scored 217 episodes and both films, mostly alone and almost entirely with synthesizers. How his music did the work the camera refused to do.

item.title: The Paranoid Style: From Pakula to the Basement
item.description: The X-Files inherited its sensibility from the conspiracy thrillers of the 1970s. A look at the films that taught it how to frame institutions, informants and the dark.

item.title: The Show That Kept Breaking Its Own Format
item.description: Unreliable narrators, time loops, videotape and near silence. The X-Files spent much of its run testing how far an episode could bend before it stopped being an episode.

item.title: In Black and White: The Post-Modern Prometheus
item.description: Chris Carter's fifth-season episode drains the color from the show and rebuilds it as a monster movie in the tradition of James Whale. Why the homage works, and what it says about the creature at its center.

item.title: Triangle and the Long Take
item.description: Chris Carter built a sixth-season episode to play as four unbroken takes, borrowing a trick from Hitchcock's Rope. A close look at what the long take does, and how it was faked.

item.title: Fight the Future: Scaling a Television Grammar to the Big Screen
item.description: In 1998 Rob Bowman took a show built on withheld images and made it carry a $60 million summer release. What survived the move to the big screen, and what the bigger frame changed.

item.title: Kim Manners and the Weekly Auteur
item.description: More than fifty episodes, from Humbug to Home to Field Trip. A portrait of the director who did more than anyone to make the show look like cinema on a television schedule.

item.title: Two Cities, Two Shows: Vancouver Gray and Los Angeles Light
item.description: After five seasons in British Columbia, the production moved to Los Angeles. The change altered everything from the weather to the color of the night, and the show adapted its storytelling to match.

item.title: Lighting the Unseen: The Flashlight Aesthetic
item.description: Network television in 1993 was built to be seen. The X-Files was built to withhold. How a weekly drama learned to treat darkness as its primary material.
